identity.title: Powered Industrial Truck Pre-Shift Inspection Log

scan.summary: This is an inspection log for a Toyota propane forklift (FL-2) at the Portland warehouse covering September 2026. The document records the results of mandatory pre-shift inspections required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7), with entries for twelve equipment items checked daily by trained operators M.C. (M. Chen) and J.R. (J. Rivera). One defect—a non-working horn on September 9—was noted and documented.
scan.freshness_note: The log ends on September 18, 2026. As of today (September 25, 2026), this log is 7 days old and shows no entries for September 19-25. Given that the truck's hour meter shows continuous operation (rising from 4,819 to 4,893 hours between the first and last dated entry), the absence of recent inspection entries is a material gap.

gaps.title: Missing inspection entries for September 19–25
gaps.description: The log ends on September 18 with no entries for the 7 most recent days of September 2026, even though the hour meter reading (4,893 hours on Sep 18) and the document's notation ('The hour meter rises between Sep 2 [4,819] and Sep 7 [4,834], which shows the truck ran on the missing days') demonstrate the truck was in continuous operation during the missing period.
gaps.fix: Complete the log by adding inspection records for every shift in which the truck was used from September 19 through September 25, 2026, with the same level of detail shown in existing entries (date, shift, hours, checklist items, operator initials, notes).
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires examination at least daily before placing in service; for round-the-clock use, after each shift.

gaps.title: Missing inspection entries for September 3–6
gaps.description: The log skips from September 2 (4,819 hours) to September 7 (4,834 hours). The document itself notes 'The hour meter rises between Sep 2 (4,819) and Sep 7 (4,834), which shows the truck ran on the missing days.' This indicates inspections should have been performed on September 3, 4, 5, and 6 but were not recorded.
gaps.fix: Reconstruct the missing entries from September 3–6 using any available records (operator time sheets, security logs, warehouse activity logs) or, if records cannot be found, document the gap formally with a note explaining why entries are missing and what effort was made to recover them.

gaps.title: Horn defect not closed out
gaps.description: On September 9, a defect was recorded: 'Horn not working' with an X mark in the Horn column. No follow-up entry appears to confirm when the horn was repaired and the truck returned to service. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires that defects 'shall be immediately reported and corrected.'
gaps.fix: Add a follow-up note to the September 9 entry or create a maintenance log entry documenting (1) when the horn repair was completed, (2) who performed it, (3) when the truck was returned to service, and (4) the date of the corrective inspection that cleared it for use.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7): 'Defects when found shall be immediately reported and corrected.'

gaps.title: Supervisor review field left blank
gaps.description: The log contains a line for 'Supervisor review: ____________________ Date: __________' which appears incomplete. No supervisor signature or review date is entered.
gaps.fix: Have a supervisor review the completed log and sign and date the review line. This creates a documentary record that a responsible party has verified the inspection log's accuracy and completeness.
gaps.citation: Industry best practice and OSHA enforcement guidance (29 CFR 1910.178 inspection logs should be reviewed and signed); not explicitly mandated in the regulation but required for defensible recordkeeping.

conditions.evidence_expected: Daily signed inspection log showing date, shift, all 12 checklist items marked (✓ for pass, X for defect), operator name or initials, notes on defects, and supervisor review. Truck hour meter reading as a cross-check of continuous operation.

conditions.title: Report defects immediately and correct them before truck returns to service
conditions.evidence_expected: Log entry with defect notation (X and note), maintenance or repair record showing corrective action, and follow-up inspection entry confirming defect resolved and truck cleared for use.

conditions.evidence_expected: Complete inspection log with no gaps, signed and dated by operators and supervisor, retained for a period sufficient to show compliance history (typically 3 years per OSHA precedent, though not explicitly mandated).

expected_missing.title: Defect closure and return-to-service documentation
expected_missing.why: When a defect is recorded (e.g., horn not working), OSHA looks for a formal record of repair completion, re-inspection, and authorization to return to service—typically a maintenance work order or defect log.

expected_missing.title: Truck-specific standard operating procedures or safe work practices manual
expected_missing.why: Chemical distribution operations using forklifts typically have or should have documented operating procedures for the warehouse, addressing load limits, aisle rules, refueling protocols, and emergency procedures.

scan.confidence_notes: I am highly confident in the identification and assessment of missing inspection entries (September 3–6 and 19–25), because the document itself provides the hour-meter evidence ('The hour meter rises between Sep 2 [4,819] and Sep 7 [4,834], which shows the truck ran on the missing days'). I am confident in the defect gap (horn not repaired/closed) because the notation is explicit and no follow-up appears. I am confident in the supervisor-review gap because the field is visibly blank. I am less confident about whether documentation of inspection logs is legally mandated (versus best practice) because OSHA's 2000 interpretation letter stated 'The standard does not require documentation of a powered industrial truck examination'; however, subsequent OSHA enforcement guidance and industry sources treat inspection logs as standard practice and necessary for defensible compliance, particularly because documentation failures are cited as a top violation. The regulation itself does not state 'document the inspection' but instead requires 'examine...do not use if defect affects safety' and 'defects when found shall be immediately reported and corrected'—which implies action, not necessarily written proof. However, modern OSHA practice and the company's own choice to keep this log mean gaps in the log create a compliance liability. I am certain that the requirement is to inspect daily (or after each shift for round-the-clock use) and not to place a truck in service if defective; I am confident that defects must be immediately reported and corrected. I did not locate Oregon-specific forklift inspection rules that would supersede federal OSHA; therefore, the analysis rests on 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7), which applies uniformly under Oregon's OSHA plan.
